sets.t: Acute and chronic pancreatitis: Essay questions
Acute and Chronic Pancreatitis: Causes, Diagnosis, Severity Scoring: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with a known history of chronic alcohol abuse and recurrent severe epigastric pain is evaluated for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Which of the following is the second most common overall cause of acute and chronic pancreatitis after gallstones?
qs.e: Gallstones are the most common cause of pancreatitis, followed closely by ethanol abuse as the second most common cause. Trauma and thiazide diuretics are less frequent causes listed in the mnemonic.

faq.a: Enteral feeding maintains gut integrity, reduces bacterial translocation and lowers infection rates.
faq.q: Why is early enteral feeding preferred over parenteral nutrition?

faq.a: Urgent ERCP is indicated for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction confirmed by imaging.
faq.q: When is ERCP indicated in acute pancreatitis?

faq.a: Yes; hereditary, autoimmune, tropical pancreatitis and obstructive causes can lead to chronic disease.
faq.q: Can chronic pancreatitis develop without alcohol use?

exam: What initial fluid regimen would you start for a patient with severe acute pancreatitis and why? — Rapid isotonic crystalloids targeting urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h to prevent hypovolemia and organ failure.

A patient with epigastric pain has normal lipase but an ultrasound shows gallstones. How do you proceed? — Consider biliary pancreatitis despite normal enzymes; arrange ERCP or surgical consult if obstruction suspected.
How does the Revised Atlanta Classification influence your management plan? — Determines need for ICU, monitoring for organ failure, and timing of interventions.
Why are routine antibiotics not recommended in the first 48 h of acute pancreatitis? — Most cases are sterile; antibiotics increase resistance and have no benefit unless infection is proven.

What are the key differences between acute necrotizing pancreatitis and a pancreatic pseudocyst on imaging? — Necrosis appears as non‑enhancing pancreatic tissue; pseudocyst is a well‑defined fluid collection with a thin wall.
Explain how you would differentiate acute pancreatitis from perforated peptic ulcer in a low‑resource setting. — Look for free air on plain X‑ray, sudden peritonitis, and absence of lipase elevation.
A chronic pancreatitis patient develops new‑onset diabetes. What pathophysiology explains this? — Progressive loss of islet β‑cells due to fibrosis and inflammation.

What lifestyle advice would you give to prevent recurrence of pancreatitis in this region? — Abstain from alcohol, avoid herbal toxins, treat gallstones, maintain healthy weight, and vaccinate against hepatitis B.
ai.title: Acute and Chronic Pancreatitis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas that can be sudden (acute) or long‑standing (chronic). It presents with abdominal pain, systemic signs and possible organ failure, and requires prompt diagnosis, severity assessment and cause‑directed management.

b: Two of three criteria confirm acute pancreatitis
Imaging (ultrasound/CT) essential when labs unavailable
sections.p: Acute pancreatitis is a sudden inflammatory response of the pancreas, diagnosed when at least two of three criteria are met: characteristic abdominal pain, serum amylase or lipase ≥3 × upper limit, or imaging showing pancreatic inflammation. Chronic pancreatitis is persistent inflammation with irreversible damage, diagnosed by imaging (calcifications, ductal changes) plus clinical features such as chronic pain or exocrine insufficiency.

t.b: Confirms pancreatic injury; ≥3 × ULN supports diagnosis – if unavailable, rely on imaging and clinical picture
Detects gallstones, pancreatic edema; useful where CT not accessible
Assesses necrosis, fluid collections; guides severity staging

b: Persistent organ failure >48 h = severe acute pancreatitis
Local complications: necrosis, pseudocyst, abscess
sections.p: Acute pancreatitis severity is graded by the Revised Atlanta Classification: mild (no organ failure, no local complications), moderately severe (transient organ failure or local complications), severe (persistent organ failure >48 h). For chronic disease, the M-ANNHEIM classification grades based on pain, imaging, endocrine/exocrine loss.

t.b: Detects organ failure; score ≥2 in any system indicates organ failure

b: Gallstones (biliary pancreatitis) – most common overall
Heavy alcohol use – especially in urban males
HIV protease inhibitors, TB drugs (rifampicin) – drug‑induced
Parasitic infections (schistosomiasis, malaria) – rare but reported
Traditional herbal remedies – toxic phytochemicals
sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings the leading causes differ from high‑income countries. Gallstone disease remains common, but alcohol, tropical infections and herbal medicines are frequent triggers.

b: Pain: constant, worsens after meals, improves leaning forward
Vomiting without bowel obstruction
Signs of systemic inflammation: fever, tachycardia
sections.p: Acute pancreatitis typically presents with sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting and a tender abdomen. Chronic pancreatitis shows recurrent epigastric pain, weight loss, steatorrhea and may have diabetes mellitus.
Choose tests that answer the key clinical questions: Is the pancreas inflamed? What is the cause? Is there organ failure? What complications exist?

t.b: Detects leukocytosis (infection) and hemoconcentration (risk of necrosis)
Assesses renal function and guides fluid resuscitation
Looks for gallstones, biliary dilatation, pancreatic swelling
Defines necrosis, fluid collections, guides intervention

b: Persistent hypotension despite fluids
Increasing abdominal distension, fever – suspect infected necrosis
Respiratory distress – possible ARDS
sections.p: Complications can be local (necrosis, pseudocyst, abscess) or systemic (organ failure, ARDS, renal failure). Early recognition of worsening organ function is vital.

b: IV crystalloids 250‑500 mL/h; target urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h
Analgesia: IV paracetamol, then opioids (morphine) – avoid NSAIDs if renal risk
Treat cause: ERCP for biliary obstruction, stop alcohol, discontinue offending drugs
Enteral nutrition within 24‑48 h if tolerated – reduces infection risk
Antibiotics only for infected necrosis (e.g., carbapenem) – not routine
sections.p: Initial care focuses on aggressive fluid resuscitation, pain control, and treating the underlying cause. Antibiotics are reserved for proven infection.

b: Pancreatic enzyme replacement for steatorrhea
Insulin therapy if new‑onset diabetes
Ultrasound surveillance for gallstones
Alcohol cessation counseling
sections.p: After discharge, monitor for recurrence, exocrine insufficiency and diabetes. Lifestyle modification and addressing biliary disease prevent future attacks.

b: Perforated ulcer – sudden pain, free air on X‑ray
Acute cholecystitis – RUQ pain, Murphy’s sign, normal lipase
sections.p: Conditions that mimic pancreatitis include perforated peptic ulcer, acute cholecystitis, mesenteric ischemia and viral hepatitis.

b: Normal lipase after 72 h does not rule out early pancreatitis
Ultrasound may miss small CBD stones – consider MRCP if available
sections.p: Serum lipase may be normal in late presentation or in chronic disease; normal ultrasound does not exclude biliary pancreatitis if stones have passed.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden collapse or loss of consciousness
New onset confusion or decreased urine output
